Input: What is a photon? Is it an object? I ask because photons are always moving at lightspeed, and no object can reach lightspeed. Well, technically, an “object” can travel at the vacuum speed of light (in fact, only at the vacuum speed of light) if it has no rest mass. In that case, the dispersion relation E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 becomes just E = p c , that is, the momentum and energy of the object are proportional to one another. Of course an “object”, or test particle, is just an abstraction of classical physics. We know that such things do not exist in a quantum reality. Nor are electrons, photons, etc., “objects”. Even in ordinary quantum mechanics, they are not miniature cannonballs: they are characterized not by positions or momenta but by states, which may translate into specific position or momentum values under the right circumstances that we perhaps call a measurement, but most of the time, the states are more complicated than that. But ordinary quantum mechanics really doesn’t know about photons. For that, we need quantum field theory, in the form of quantum electrodynamics. We know from Maxwell’s theory that far away from charges, in otherwise empty space, influences in the electromagnetic field travel as plane waves at the invariant velocity c . (This invariance is what inspired special relativity after all). In the quantum field theory, the energy of these waves can only increase or decrease by predetermined units, or quanta. When something interacts with the electromagnetic field, this increase or decrease registers, or can be interpreted as, the emission or the absorption of a particle. We call these quanta or particles photons. So what travels at the vacuum speed of light is, well, light, electromagnetic waves far away from sources (charges). Particle-like behavior is observed when these waves are emitted or absorbed, leading us to the mental model of thinking of a ray of light as a bunch of photons (which is misleading since we know for a fact since the beginning of the 19th century, the famous Arago-spot and all, that light is a wave, not corpuscular in nature). Short story: Particles in quantum field theory are not miniature cannonballs, but unit excitations of fields. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can you explain the difference between "dark matter" and "dark energy"? What is the proportion of each in our universe? Certainly. It has to do with pressure. Cosmologists are simple-minded folks. They realized that on the largest of scales, the universe is rather uniform: it is more or less, on average, the same everywhere and it has no preferred direction. Which means, among other things, that its content can be modeled as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: a medium that has no shear, no viscosity, only density and pressure, and its pressure is independent of direction. But how much pressure? Well, for something this simple, there’s a rather simplistic mathematical representation: the “equation of state”, w = p / ρ . Here, p is the pressure and ρ is the energy density. (Remember, energy is just mass times speed-of-light squared, so energy density vs. mass density really are the same thing.) The beauty of this expression is that p and ρ are measured using the same units. How come, you may wonder? Well… pressure is force divided by area. Energy is force times distance; and volume is area times length (i.e., distance). So energy density would be (force times distance) divided by (area times distance), which is force divided by area… same as pressure. Therefore, the ratio w of these two is just a pure number, a “dimensionless” quantity. But what is it? Well… what if there is no pressure? That would be w = 0. Cosmologists call this “dust”. (Did I mention they’re simple-minded?) As it turns out, most ordinary matter is well approximated as “dust”. Only immensely hot matter, in which particles zip about at relativistic speeds, will have a value that substantially differs from zero. How substantially? In the extreme limit of an “ultrarelativistic gas”, w = 1 / 3. But the equations actually allow more extreme values, values outside the range between 0 and 1/3. In fact, we can have w = 1. Beyond that, w > 1 will not work as it implies a medium in which sound travels faster than the vacuum speed of light! But anything below 1 is okay. In fact, w can be negative! Yes, negative pressure. (Think about it: when particles of a gas repel each other, we have positive pressure. So if they were to attract each other, “clump”, that would be negative pressure.) As a matter of fact, any value w ≥ − 1 will do. (Stuff with w < − 1 would yield an unstable universe.) OK, one more piece to the puzzle: as the universe expands, the energy density of this stuff changes. But the energy density also involves the energy of interactions between particles of this stuff. For this reason, only the energy density of “dust” will change as the inverse of volume. In fact, at one extreme of the scale, at w = − 1 , the energy density of this stuff remains constant even as the universe expands! This is important, as you shall see in a moment. So then… our postulate is that the universe consists of such an isotropic perfect fluid, or perhaps a mix of isotropic perfect fluids. But what kind? How much? Well… we look at observation. The age of the universe. The statistical distribution of matter. Minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background. Distant supernovas. Long story short, we find that the universe “works” if it consists of roughly 30% “dust” and 70% of stuff with w = − 1 , together making up 100% of the so-called “critical density”, which is needed for a universe in which the geometry of space is Euclidean on average. The problem is that the actual stuff that we see: Stars, gas, dust (actual dust, not “dust”), etc., amounts to only about 4%. The remaining 96% has to be something else. We call the missing 26% of “dust” “dark matter”; and the missing 70% of stuff with w = − 1 “dark energy”. There is a lot of speculation as to what this “dark matter” and this “dark energy” are. But we don’t know. So far, experiments designed to detect these mediums directly all came up empty. We infer their existence from gravity and cosmological observations; we have not seen either. However, what we do know if our hypotheses are correct is that as the universe ages and expands, “dust” gets diluted; stuff with w = − 1 does not. So over time, “dark energy” dominates. In fact, it already does, which means that (due to its negative pressure) it is already accelerating the rate at which the universe expands. So there. That’s what dark matter and dark energy are, and this is pretty much all that we actually know about them. There’s plenty of speculation, to be sure, but speculation, even informed speculation, is not knowledge. Oh, how nice. Quora again offered some Stable Diffusion illustrations to accompany my answer. Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

What effect does gravity have on a photon moving directly away from a massive object? You stumbled upon one of the three “classical tests” of general relativity theory proposed by Einstein when the theory was new. The other two are the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of rays of light by a gravitating body. This one, however, is about redshift. Namely that rays of light, photons, arriving from a “deep gravitational well”, will appear to have lost energy. Key to understanding this is gravitational time dilation: remembering that a “perfect clock” appears to tick more slowly when in a gravitational field, compared to an identical clock that is far from any gravitational source. So then, imagine a ray of light, say, a very blue/violet ray of light with a wavelength of 400 nm leaving the surface of a compact, heavy object. Suppose that the object is so heavy, clocks there appear to tick at a rate that is 2/3rd the rate of a clock in deep space, far from sources of gravitation. That 400 nm light ray corresponds to an electromagnetic field that oscillates 750 trillion times a second (750 THz). That is, 750 trillion oscillations while a clock near the light source counts 1 second. Now imagine someone in deep space detecting this light ray. That person uses his own clock to measure time. and his own clock appears to tick faster. While the clock on the surface of the object counted 1 second, this clock in deep space will have counted 3/2 times 1 second, which is to say, one and a half seconds. So it takes one and a half seconds to receive those 750 trillion oscillations. Which means that in one second, this detector will have seen only 500 trillion oscillations. That is to say, it will have observed that light ray at 500 THz, not 750 THz. The corresponding wavelength, then, is not 400 nm but 600 nm. What started off as very blue light arrives at the detector as light that appears very much more like orange. And this, then, is the effect of gravity on a photon. As it climbs out of the “gravity well”, the photon loses energy, which is to say, its characteristic frequency shifts down, the corresponding wavelength increasing. The distortion in space and time created by the mass of the Earth is extremely small, less than one part in a billion. Isn't that too little to make things accelerate at 9.8m/s2 towards the ground? It is true that the change in observed spacetime geometry, time dilation in particular, here on the surface of the Earth is tiny. It is characterized by the dimensionless quantity G M / c 2 r ≃ 7 × 10 − 10 so indeed, less than one part in a billion. However, gravitational acceleration is a tad larger: it is c 2 / r times this quantity, which indeed comes to about 9.8 meters per seconds squared. So no, that tiny quantity is not too little, nor is it too great. It is precisely what it takes to accelerate things here on the surface of the Earth at one standard gravity. But one standard gravity is a tiny, tiny, acceleration when you consider more extreme cosmic objects. On the surface of something like a neutron star, gravitational acceleration is tens of billions of times greater. That puts neutron stars deeply in the relativistic regime insofar as gravitation is concerned. In contrast, here on the Earth, the consequences of relativity theory amount to, you guessed it, typically one part in a billion or thereabouts. Is it possible to use telescopes to observe the event horizon and beyond of a black hole, or does the gravity of the black hole absorb all light before it reaches us? Here is the thing about black holes: No photon ever leaves the event horizon. This would be true even if we had pre-formed, “primordial” black holes in this universe, with fully formed event horizons. This is the very nature of an event horizon, nothing, not even light, can ever come from one. Add to this the fact that an actual, astrophysical black hole that forms as a result of gravitational collapse never really completes the process. Its event horizon remains forever in the future of any observer outside. So to “see” its event horizon, you’d need not a telescope but first and foremost, a time machine, to bring a signal from the future to the present! In short, no. Not even with an all-powerful telescope can you see what’s not actually there, namely light leaving a black hole’s event horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

The movie Odds and Evens (És Megint Dühbe Jövünk in Hungarian) can be a famous Italian-made movie. What is your opinion on this movie? Do you also like the English dub as well? Wow. I have not heard anyone mention this 1978 movie in decades. The late Bud Spencer (born Carlo Pedersoli) and Terence Hill (Mario Girotti). A sequel of sorts (at least in spirit: the Hungarian-language titles — literally translated as “Otherwise we get mad!” and “We’re getting mad again!” — reflected this) to their 1974 Watch Out, We’re Mad!, it was a hilarious comedy, extremely popular in Hungary when I was a young teen. Are these good films? Well, are spaghetti Westerns any good? These films are of a different genre, but in my mind, they represent the same era of Italian filmmaking. No, they are not classics. No Fellini, not even Once Upon A Time in the West. But they were memorable comedies, and as young teens living behind the former Iron Curtain, we just loved them. Anyone my age who grew up in Hungary likely remembers them well. Just checked and Watch Out, We’re Mad! has a respectable rating of 7.3 on IMDB. Odds and Evens is rated 7.1. What can I say? They were fun films. I have fond memories of them 40-odd years later. That’s more than I can say about most films that I saw in my life, so there. I never saw either with English dubbing, so I really have no idea. Hungarian dubbing back in the 1970s tended to be fairly good, though I guess it also helped that we lived in a far less interconnected world, so watching characters on the silver screen, conversing in Hungarian in an obviously foreign environment, felt far less uncanny back then. These days, I avoid dubbing whenever possible; when I watch foreign films, I always opt for subtitles if I can.

Does dark matter convert into energy like baryonic matter (E=MC^2)? If so, what type of energy (not electromagnetic or dark energy)? Contrary to millions of popular accounts that suggest otherwise (usually to dazzle their readership), the equation, E = m c 2 , is absolutely not about converting anything into anything. Here is the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduced this equation in its modern interpretation (the correct one, not the misunderstood reinterpretations): Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? (Does the Inertia of a Body Depend upon its Energy-Content, Annalen der Physik, 18:639, 1905). Let’s look at the title more closely. Inertia of course means inertial mass, the resistance of a body to acceleration. This is the mass m that appears in Newton’s second law, F = m a . Einstein’s question, which he answers affirmatively in the body of the paper, is whether the inertia of a body is determined by whatever energies are “stored” inside that body. Any by “energy”, we don’t mean anything mysterious. There really are only two types of energy worth considering. One is the energy of motion: kinetic energy. The other is the energy associated with positions (where a body is): potential energy. This is about how bodies relate to one another, attraction and repulsion and the associated energy. A special case is rest mass, which can be seen as a body interacting with itself. In quantum field theory, “particles” are in a sense illusions: what are real are the quantum fields. The quantum fields can gain energy from interacting with other quantum fields, and when they gain energy, it comes in the form of discrete lumps, “excitations”. These excitations may be detected in the right experiments as discrete particles. This is how particles are “created”. So when two quantum fields interact, their kinetic energies can transform, create new excitations, and new “particles” are born, so long as all other conservation laws are satisfied. It is not possible to create a single electron this way; that would violate charge conservation. But it is possible to create an electron-positron pair, in the right experimental setup, by allowing other fields carrying lots and lots of kinetic energy interact with the electron field (not to be confused with the electromagnetic field, the quanta of which are the photons). But it requires interaction. So moving on to dark matter: the standard “cold/collisionless dark matter”, or CDM model involves dark matter that does not interact (or if it does, only very weakly) with itself or with baryonic matter. So it does not matter how much kinetic energy is present in the form of dark matter, if it cannot transfer that energy to the Standard Model fields that constitute normal (baryonic) matter. Finally, one more comment on the terminology. The expression “dark energy” suggests some other type of energy! It is not. Words mislead us, especially when the jargon of a field or profession alters meaning. Theoretical physics has quite a few examples: the “vacuum speed of light” may not be the speed at which light travels (e.g., if we allow photons to be massive), gauge theories have nothing to do with gauges, modern particle physics is really the physics of interacting fields with “particles” only an afterthought and, well, dark energy is not energy, really, but a “perfect fluid” (which is not really fluid, lol) a medium that has uniform density and pressure with no shear or viscosity. In particular, dark energy is a perfect fluid with very large negative pressure. Not some mysterious form of “energy”, although of course, like all forms of matter, it has energy-content. Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take? Well, for starters, even if there was a known method to compress matter in such small quantities to densities far exceeding the density even in the interior of the densest neutron star, it would likely require energy far in excess of the 1 gram rest mass-energy of the matter that we started with. OK, so maybe we can start with 0.1 grams or whatever, so in the end, we create a 1 gram black hole after investing an insane amount of energy by a yet-to-be-discovered process. Well, that black hole would not last very long. It would release all its energy in 0.0000000000000000000000000465 seconds, give or take, mostly in the form of gamma radiation that would be at least ten orders of magnitude more energetic than the particle energies in the Large Hadron Collider. These gamma photons would of course be absorbed by whatever is nearby, resulting in extreme heat and ultimately a thermal explosion with a power comparable to that of the Hiroshima bomb. Kaboom! But suppose we got this all wrong and there is no Hawking radiation; so once created, our 1 gram black hole is eternal. It would indeed fall through the floor and… well, not so much sink as fall freely towards the center of the Earth, interacting only infrequently with the atoms it runs across during its journey. Why? Because it would be insanely, insanely small. Something like 15 orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. And its supposedly enormous gravity? Not that enormous if you think about it unless you get very, very, very close. You’d have to be within less than one tenth of a micron from this black hole to experience 1 g acceleration. Would this 1 gram black hole accrete matter? Yes, it would. I calculated its so-called Bondi accretion rate assuming it’s sinking in a nonrelativistic medium with a density ten times that of water and a speed of sound of 1000 m/s, which is probably not a gross misrepresentation of the Earth’s interior. Long story short, assuming I used my calculator correctly, it would take roughly 10 billion times the present age of the universe… for the 1 g black hole to double in size and become a 2 g black hole.

Considering that the event horizon around Sagittarius A black hole reaches millions of degrees in temperature, how far away from the black hole itself would you have to be for the temperature to be a comfortable 70°F? The Hawking-temperature associated with the Sgr A* event horizon region is not millions of degrees. It’s not even single-digit degrees. It’s a small fraction of a trillionth of a degree kelvin above absolute zero. The accretion disk (rapidly swirling, infalling material) around Sgr A* can reach millions of degrees due to internal friction and collisions. At no distance from it would you enjoy “a comfortable 70 F”, though. The bulk thermal radiation coming from this accretion disk is in the form of hard X-rays. We can calculate how far you’d have to be from it to receive a flux that would be consistent with being in a room with walls at 70 F, but I assure you, it would not be comfortable at all. Rather, though the energy deposited by those X-rays may keep you warm, your body would rapidly suffer irreversible damage as it absorbs such quantities of ionizing radiation, breaking up molecular bonds, destroying your cells’ DNA. Can you explain why the pressure inside of a black hole becomes infinite? The interior solution describing a collapsing astrophysical object turns out to be the same set of equations that would describe a collapsing cosmos. A hapless observer who found himself falling into a black hole, after crossing the event horizon, would find himself in such a collapsing “mini-Universe”. Depending on the size of this mini-Universe (determined by the amount of matter that fell, and will ever fall, into it), it may take anywhere from a millisecond to many hours, but the mini-Universe collapses. The observer would not live to see this, as ever increasing tidal forces would rip his body apart before the end. But that end (at least for a spherically symmetric black hole) inevitably happens: the famed “singularity” is not some bad spot that you can bypass by clever maneuvering, but a future moment in time at which (insofar as this mini-Universe is concerned) time itself comes to an end. So it’s not so much that pressure, density, etc., become infinite at this moment but rather, this moment literally is not part of existence: Whatever is inside the mini-Universe ceases to exist at this point. For outside observers, however, none of this ever happens. Even the event horizon itself remains forever in their future. Only by falling through it can the event horizon be experienced. That is the “classical” picture anyway. If we account for quantum physics, the answer is, we don’t really know what happens. In the absence of a quantum gravity theory, we can only take educated guesses, invoking what is known as the “semiclassical approximation”. One possibility (if you asked me, I think it’s the most likely one) is that the collapse never even happens as the black hole evaporates before its event horizon forms. In which case, there is no “inside” at all. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why were the breakthroughs in the development of physics from 1900 to 1935 far greater than subsequent period? It seems that those 35 years were the period of the greatest explosion in the development of physics in the entire science history. Is the premise of this question really valid? Permit me to challenge it. Certainly, the first one third of the 20th century saw not one but two extraordinary revolutions in physics, the development of relativity theory and that of the quantum theory. But similar, profound revolutions have taken place previously. Perhaps the biggest, I’d argue, something even more profound than the development of quantum physics and relativity, was the shift from the Aristotelian to the modern view of the physical world. In Aristotle’s view, the celestial spheres and the terrestrial sphere were governed by different laws. In the celestial spheres, motion was eternal. In the terrestrial sphere, motion was temporary, always coming to an end without a mover of some sort. The celestial spheres were “perfect”, unchanging, whereas the terrestrial sphere was subject to decay. With the work of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and ultimately, Newton, this was replaced by a world view in which the same fundamental laws governed heaven and earth. And these fundamental laws became precise, expressed using the language of mathematics, in particular the mathematics of infinitesimal changes, i.e., calculus. I cannot stress how fundamental this shift was to the development of modern science. Compared to this, the birth of quantum physics and the theory of relativity are… well, almost child’s play. Moving on, in the late 18th and the 19th century, another groundbreaking development took place: the advent of the “action principle”, the idea that the equations that govern a physical system can be derived by minimizing the “action”, a mathematical expression that characterizes a system’s evolution over time. It is difficult to stress just how critical the action principle has become in nearly all branches of fundamental physics: It governs mechanical systems, both particles and continua; classical field theories (electromagnetism and gravitation); and it forms an absolutely crucial foundation for the quantum theory. And no, physics did not come to an end in the 1930s. What was yet to happen was the development of quantum field theory, including non-Abelian theories, the modern understanding of the role intrinsic symmetries play in the behavior of quantum fields, ultimately leading to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics, a model that (as far as we know) accurately describes all the fundamental building blocks of the universe excluding gravitation. So yes, the first third of the 20th century was a remarkable period in physics, when two major revolutions took place at the same time. But that does not mean that similar, profound shifts in our understanding have not taken place before or after. And not just in physics; how about, for instance, biology, the understanding of DNA and the molecular foundations of genetics, that took place in the 1950s? It is perhaps true that fundamental physics has been a bit “stuck” in the past 50 years, not so much for lack of ideas but for lack of experimental evidence: Without hints from Nature, we can’t tell which approach, e.g., makes better sense as we try to improve the compatibility of the quantum theory and gravitation. Even so, look at the application side of things. It wasn’t that long ago that things like a blue LED seemed like unachievable “holy grails” in semiconductor technology, yet here we are, chances are you are reading this on a device with an OLED display, sitting in a room lit by a high power white LED lightbulb. Or not. Maybe you are not reading my silly words at all, consulting instead with a large language model, a culmination of some 70 years of research that began with simple “neural networks” designed to simulate the basic structure of neurons in the animal brain? So breakthroughs happen all the time. The first 30-odd years of the 20th century must have been an amazing time to be alive for a physicist, but you know what, I much rather do physics in 2024, with all the knowledge we have since added in the intervening century. What is the current understanding of dark energy using general relativity? Can GR provide any insights into the nature of this mysterious phenomenon in our universe? To answer this question, I must first point out a very important fact: General relativity is not a theory of matter. It is a theory of gravitation. Insofar as matter is concerned, general relativity simply states that matter “couples universally and minimally” to the gravitational field: in technical terms, this is written as T μ ν = − ( 2 / √ − g ) δ S m / δ g μ ν , which is a mathematical equation that essentially tells us that the stress-energy-momentum of matter serves as the source of the gravitational field. But as to what that matter is, on that subject general relativity remains silent. That is not to say that we cannot speculate about the nature of matter. In particular, we often postulate that matter, whatever it is made of, behaves on large scales as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: that is to say, a medium entirely characterized by its density and pressure. (There is no directionality, no stresses, no viscosity, just density and pressure). A perfect fluid is easily characterized then by the ratio of its pressure and its energy density. In any sensible system of units, these two quantities are measured using the same units. Energy is force time distance, volume is area times distance, therefore energy density: energy divided by volume, is the same as pressure: force divided by area. Which means that the ratio of these two quantities is a pure number, not dependent on the choice of units. This number is zero for stuff with no pressure (sometimes called “dust”). It’s very close to zero for most “normal” matter. For a relativistic gas (gas so hot, its particles move around at nearly the speed of light) the ratio is 1/3. But really, a perfect fluid makes sense with that ratio being anywhere between -1 (yes, negative pressure) and +1. (Less than -1 means an unstable cosmos, more than +1 means a medium in which sound travels faster than light.) The rest is easy, so to speak. When we look at astronomical observations on cosmological scales, we find that the data can be modeled using general relativity if the universe is made up of 30% “dust” and 70% stuff with the aforementioned ratio being -1. We call this perfect fluid “dark energy”. Of the 30% dust, about 4% is “normal” matter (not exactly dust, but close, as most normal matter is not relativistic). The rest is “dark matter”. We have no idea what “dark matter” and “dark energy” are, although there are many proposals. The only thing we know about them is that they are, well, “dark” although “transparent” might be closer to the truth: They do not interact with (emit, absorb, block or reflect) light, indeed they do not interact with matter at all (or if they do, they do so very, very weakly). That’s all we really know about this “dark” stuff. Everything else is conjecture, since none of this “dark” stuff has ever been observed. And it is of course still eminently possible that none of this “dark” stuff exists, but rather, our theories are on the wrong track. In any case, the answer, if it comes, won’t come from general relativity. It will either be in a form that modifies general relativity (and does away with the need for “dark” things) or in a form of a better theory of matter, hopefully one with directly testable predictions so that it can be validated by observation.

Since we cannot observe an object crossing an event horizon, does this mean we cannot ever observe an object expanding out of the observable universe? Will it just get more and more redshifted forever? Meaning there is no “un observable” universe? Yes, to the first part of the question. If you were to watch a distant galaxy, you would never see it cross your cosmological event horizon. Its light would simply become more and more redshifted. But no, that does not mean that there is no “un observable” universe. It simply implies that there are parts of the universe that almost certainly exist, but which we cannot ever observe. And that’s why I added the “almost certainly” qualifier. For all I know, just beyond the limits of the observable universe, everything changes, it’s all dancing pink unicorns in whipped cream or something equally silly. If that is the case, we would never know. However, if we assume that by and large, the same rules govern the universe everywhere, including beyond the limits of its observable bits, then pink unicorns are out, and in all likelihood, the universe is still its same old boring self, mostly empty, with galaxies and stars and planets floating around in the void, even far beyond the boundaries of the observable universe. What is the difference in difficulty between quantum mechanics and quantum field theory? Why is one considered easier than the other? I don’t know about “easier”… understanding the quantum world is not easy, because it does not lend itself to intuition. This obstacle is the same whether you do field theory or particle theory. A particle theory in classical mechanics deals with the positions and momenta of particles subject to forces, which may be represented by potentials. We may turn a classical particle theory into a quantum theory by replacing positions and momenta with abstract entities that do not commute under multiplication. These abstract entities, “q-numbers” as Dirac called them, can be represented by matrices or by operators acting on some function, which represents the state of the system. The resulting equation (Schrödinger’s) is already known as a wave equation (that is to say, its solutions are typically wave-like solutions) so the function representing the state of the system is called the wavefunction. In the standard (Copenhagen) interpretation, we view this wavefunction as a probability density, as the squared norm of this function can be used to calculate the outcome of measurements, taken by (idealized, hypothesized) classical instruments. When we take the Schrödinger equation for a specific system known from classical mechanics, the harmonic oscillator, the solutions we get have a peculiar property: Only certain, discrete levels of energy represent valid solutions. This is an example of a system that became “quantized”. (As I hope it is obvious from the discussion so far, not all quantum systems are “quantized” in this sense of the word! E.g., a free particle can have any energy, its energy levels are not “quantized” even in the quantum theory.) So what is a field? In classical physics, a field is a physical entity that is present at every location at every moment in time. The field’s value may change from point to point or moment to moment, but it is governed by some sensible equation. In particular, we can assign for instance a “momentum density” to the field at various points, and use it to study how the field evolves over time. But there is one other thing that we can do with a field: Express it as a sum of elementary sine waves by means of a Fourier-transform. And elementary sine waves are basically harmonic oscillators! This, then, opens a path towards quantizing fields: If we can express a field as a (potentially infinite) sum of harmonic oscillators, we know already how to quantize harmonic oscillators. There, we have a quantum field theory. Now each of these harmonic oscillators has discrete energy levels. Its energy can only go up or down by set units. The premise of quantum field theory is that it is these discrete units that we perceive as particles. So when we say, for instance, that the electromagnetic field is “quantized” and its quanta are the “photons”, this is exactly what happens: Each “photon” is a unit excitation of one of the (infinitely many) harmonic oscillators that make up the electromagnetic field in this representation. Why do we do this, you might wonder? Well, quantum field theory has two very important properties that make all this effort worthwhile. First, as it allows the field to gain, or lose, excitations when it interacts with other fields, it lets us model particle creation and annihilation. No quantum particle theory can do that. And of course we do observe in Nature particle creation and annihilation all the time. Secondly, a quantum particle theory is known to violate causality. No matter how clever we are, constructing a relativistic version of quantum mechanics, there is always some “probability leakage” (my expression), some small but nonvanishing probability of an event influencing another event faster than light, or worse, backwards in time. In turn, quantum field theory is strictly causal: Such acausal interactions are exactly canceled out by the theory, no “leakage”. So why do people think quantum field theory is only an “effective” theory then? Well, I mentioned those pesky harmonic oscillators. Their energy levels are not only discrete, their lowest energy level is not zero! Now this is not a problem when all you have is one harmonic oscillator. But a field consists of infinitely many of them. Infinitely many oscillators means an infinite amount of “zero point energy”, which does not make sense. It turns out that in many cases, these infinities can be dealt with using a reasonably robust mathematical procedure, allowing us to extract finite numbers that describe actual observable results. The mathematical process is called renormalization. But not all quantum field theories are renormalizable, and in particular, gravity is a theory that becomes non-renormalizable as a quantum field theory. Gravity becomes important for quantum systems at the “Planck scale”. So it is widely thought that at that energy scale, quantum field theory ceases to work, and something more fundamental is needed. So there, that sums it up. Does this make quantum field theory harder than quantum mechanics? Well, it certainly builds upon quantum mechanics. But in a sense, it “completes” quantum mechanics in a very sensible way, so perhaps conceptually it is easier, even if its mathematical toolset may be a tad more complicated. Then again, with the problem of renormalizability… perhaps it’s harder after all. You be the judge. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without? As a driver? Absolutely, I’d use my seatbelt. I’ve been in accidents. (Fortunately none involving personal injury to anyone). Therefore, I know both from theory and from practice what it means when the seatbelt not only keeps you safer (which you may not care about) but keeps you behind the wheel. Which means that if, after the accident, the vehicle is still (somewhat) controllable, you might regain control. You may be able to stop the vehicle before it causes additional harm to others. You may still be able to steer, preventing injury to others. All this is kind of hard to do if you have already left the vehicle through the windshield as a wingless projectile, or ended up on the rear seat as the vehicle spun about. Questions like this remind me of questions I sometimes see concerning religion: “If you are an atheist, what stops you from committing certain sins?” Here are a few words or phrases to contemplate: “Empathy”. “Compassion”. “Social responsibility”. In other words, even if you don’t care about your own safety in an accident, you could still consider that a seat belt might help you keep others, including quite possibly your own loved ones in that vehicle, safer. I know, I know, outlandish commie propaganda and all but hey, even Ayn Rand advocated enlightened self-interest: that is to say, the recognition that even if your own well-being takes precedence over that of the others, acting at least occasionally in the interests of the group might actually be beneficial to the individual…

Is it possible for an object to become heavier than anything else in existence, including black holes, if it reaches lightspeed through acceleration? Objects do not become heavier by acceleration. Objects gain kinetic energy by acceleration, as measured in the reference frame of other objects that do not accelerate along with the object in question. Decades ago, relativity texts often introduced the concept of “relativistic mass”, which lumped together the (intrinsic) rest mass of the moving object with its (observer-dependent) kinetic energy. Fortunately, this concept is not much used anymore and, well, good riddance, because it led to a lot of misunderstandings. So no, an object will not become heavier no matter how close to the vacuum speed of light it moves in some observer’s reference frame. (Keep in mind that motion is always relative: objects move relative to other objects, in their own reference frames they are always at rest.) Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Let me describe to you an imaginary journey into a classical black hole. ("Classical" in the sense that I am ignoring quantum effects, notably Hawking radiation, which might even prevent the black hole from forming in the first place. So let's say that you are not only in a very good spaceship, but you are also almost imprevious to extreme acceleration and extreme tidal forces. You hope into your spaceship, travel to the nearest collapsing sphere of matter that will ultimately form a black hole, and choose a trajectory that will end up in the black hole as well. If the collapsing matter has negligible pressure, its collapse will not be slowed down by any means. Yet to those on the outside, the process of the collapse will appear to slow as the cloud gets close to becoming a black hole. That is because of extreme gravitational time dilation: anything that happens near this collapsing cloud of matter will appear in slow motion to anyone far away. Not to you though. You will find that you will approach the surface of this collapsing cloud, but you won't quite be able to catch up with it. Meanwhile, however, as the gravitational field gets stronger, you will notice that what was a spherical surface below now appears to "curl up" on the sides. That is because of the gravitational deflection of light: many light rays that start off going upward will be bent downward, so they will appear to hit your eyeball from above! What was one a surface below begins to form a wall around you, and soon enough, it will feel like you are in a vertical tunnel, or well, its opening rapidly closing above you. Suppose you chicken out at the very last split second, punch a button, and with your Extremely Powerful Rocket [tm] you escape. Much to your surprise, you'll find that what has taken only a few seconds by your reckoning took a year outside. Or a thousand years. Or a quintillion years. This is why those on the outside can never be sure that the black hole even forms; no matter how long they wait, there's a chance that you re-emerge. It's only a question of how close you cut it before punching out. But what if you don't? Well, there will be a moment when the matter above your head closes up. There is no opening anymore. No walls really, either, as this is also the moment when you caught up with all the collapsing matter after all, so now you are inside the cloud. Inside a homogeneous (same everywhere) isotropic (no preferred direction) cloud of matter that forms a collapsing mini-universe, in which you are trapped. The moment when this happened is the event horizon. NOT a place. Not a location to which you can return. A moment — now a moment in the past — of time. So without a time machine, you are doomed. This mini-universe is a collapsing universe, the exact opposite of the kind of universe we seem to live in, outside of the black hole. Second by second, minute by minute it becomes denser. (Or millisecond by millisecond, if the collapsing cloud weighed "only" as much as, say, three times the mass of our Sun, or a million times the mass of the Earth.) Did I say same everywhere? Yes, I did. I meant it. There is no center, no edge of this cloud. This entire self-enclosed mini-universe is filled with matter everywhere. And you have very little time left. And perhaps that's when you recall something that you may have heard before in the past: The so-called "singularity" is not some center either. Rather, it is the moment in time when density, pressure, temperature, etc., everything in this mini-universe diverges, becomes infinite. The mini-universe ceases to exist (it's called geodesic incompleteness). Along with you, of course. Think this scenario through and now contemplate if it is even meaningful to talk about "destroying" a black hole. What exactly would that "destruction" do? Remember, to those on the outside, the black hole does not even exist yet, no matter how long they wait. Whereas for those on the inside, the black hole is the ONLY thing that exists, and its fate is sealed: soon enough everything, including time itself (!) comes to an end in this doomed mini-universe.

A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it? Actually, when you bring a piece of iron to a magnet, the system has less energy when the iron is closer to the magnet. You need to invest energy, do work to separate the iron from the magnet. The amount of energy is usually minuscule so it is not something we can measure, but to offer an intuition: Suppose you have a magnet and you release a piece of iron nearby. The magnet attracts it: the piece of iron accelerates, gaining kinetic energy at the expense of losing potential energy. The overall energy-content of the system remains the same. Then finally, the piece of iron hits the magnet and stops moving. Its kinetic energy now transforms into the random motion of its and the magnet’s molecules, i.e., it gets converted into heat. That heat is then radiated away into the environment as both the piece of iron and the magnet cool down th ambient temperature. The amount of energy lost by way of that waste heat radiated away is precisely the amount by which the mass-energy of the system decreases. Of course as I said, the amount is minuscule. Far, far less than what we could possibly measure even with our most sensitive instruments. However, similar processes that go on either on the nuclear scale (much large energies) or simply on a much larger mass scale (e.g., astrophysical systems) do have measurable properties that explicitly confirm this description. Going back to the piece of iron and the magnet, to remove the piece of iron the process needs to be reversed. A force must be applied to separate the piece of iron from the magnet and move it some distance away. The work done by this force is now the potential energy of the system, i.e., its ability to make the piece of iron move again if it were to be released, allowed again to accelerate towards the magnet. Can you explain the concept of dark energy in the Big Bang theory? Is it considered a part of inflation? Not precisely part of inflation, but related. The standard cosmological model assumes a universe that is the same everywhere (homogeneous) and has no preferred direction (isotropic). All forms of “matter” (and by “matter”, we mean anything and everything that’s not empty space) would be in the form of “isotropic perfect fluids”: that is to say, mediums that are characterized by its mass density ρ and pressure p . The ratio of energy density and pressure is a pure number: w = p / c 2 ρ . This “equation of state” characterizes the medium. The number w can be anything between -1 and +1 (yes, this includes negative pressure). It is substantially different from zero only for “relativistic” forms of matter: ordinary matter is well described by w = 0 , which is to say, its pressure is much, much less than its energy density. (Values below -1 would yield an unstable universe; values over +1 would yield a speed of sound that exceeds the vacuum speed of light, violating causality.) So then, the question becomes: What mixture of such perfect fluids yield the observed properties of the universe? When we take the totality of observations into account, we find that observable results — including the cosmic microwave background, its minute fluctuations, the large-scale distribution of matter, the luminosity-redshift relationship of Type Ia supernovae, and a host of other observations — can be best modeled if the universe is assumed to be “spatially flat”, with 30% of all matter in the form of w = 0 “dust”, and 70% in the form of w = − 1 “dark energy”. Ordinary matter amounts to only about 4%, so the remaining 26% of “dust” is assumed to be something invisible, dubbed “dark matter”. Though there are plenty of theories, we have no idea what either of these “dark” things really are; the names are basically placeholders representing our ignorance. There is a curious point concerning matter with significant, relativistic pressure. For ordinary matter, its gravitation is determined by the mass density ρ . However, when relativistic pressure is present, it must be included as a source of gravitation: we end up with ρ + 3 p / c 2 as the source. For dark energy, w = − 1 , this implies that gravitation will be proportional to − 2 ρ , that is to say, it is repulsive! This is why the presence of dark energy actually pushes stuff in distant parts of the universe away from each other, accelerating the rate at which the universe continues to expand. Note that this is not inflation. However, inflation is related. It was supposed to happen in the very early universe, when something akin to dark energy dominated the universe, accelerating its expansion for a very brief but significant period of time. Whatever was the source of that large negative pressure, however, is supposed to have undergone some kind of phase transition, its negative pressure vanishing. Afterwards, the rate of expansion began to decrease and continued to decrease for roughly 9 billion years, before (ordinary and dark) matter became sufficiently dilute so that dark energy became dominant, and the rate of expansion began to increase again. Bottom line: though the mechanisms are closely related, do not confuse inflation (rapid expansion in the extreme early universe) with acceleration (the universe slowly shifting from a decelerating to an accelerating rate of expansion in the past 4–5 billion years). Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. How is communication maintained with the Voyager space probe despite its distance from Earth? Is there a relay system in place for this purpose? No relay systems are involved. They would not be practical. The Voyagers have a 3.66 meter parabolic reflector, serving as a high-gain antenna for both transmission and reception. They can transmit in the S-band (2.3 GHz) or X-band (8.4 GHz) though I understand that nowadays, only the X-band downlink is used. The downlink power of the traveling wave tube (TWT) amplifier is, I believe, maximum 19 watts. Utilizing the smaller, 34-m receiving antennas of NASA’s deep space network (DSN), it is possible to get a downlink data rate of 160 bps (bits per second), or maybe (starting this year, for Voyager 1) 40 bps. With the DSN’s large, 70-m antennas, a downlink rate of 600 bps is still possible. Uplink is accomplished in the S-band (2.1 GHz) using a 20 kW transmitter via the 70-m antennas (the DSN also has the capability to transmit at 400 kW, but I understand it is not needed for Voyager). Cannot find the typical data rate but it seems to be a few hundred bps. Voyager 2, in particular, has a quirk: due to a minor on-board failure, it is very sensitive to the frequency of the carrier that it receives, so uplinks are usually repeated with very minor frequency adjustments, transmitted several times to make sure that the spacecraft receives the command. Even when there are no actual commands to send, the spacecraft routinely receive “command loss timer reset” commands, which basically inform them that the uplink works; otherwise, the spacecraft might decide that it has lost communication with the Earth. So yes, it is all direct communication. Relays do not work, really. Apart from the impracticality of placing relay satellites at large interplanetary distances, there’s also the consideration that whereas here on the Earth, we can build 70-m antennas, power them with transmitters rated at tens or hundreds of kilowatts, and use ultra-sensitive receivers cooled to near absolute zero, these luxuries are not available in deep space. So a direct communications link that makes use of the abundant resources here on the Earth is almost always preferable to a relay link. (Relay links still make sense, e.g., when we have a robot on the surface of a planet and a relay satellite orbiting that planet.) Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? The graviton is difficult to detect because gravity is very weak, which means that the probability of any particular graviton to interact with matter is very, very, very low. The late Freeman Dyson in his 2012 Poincaré Prize lecture calculated that the Sun, in addition to the humongous amount of thermal energy it emits as electromagnetic radiation (mostly light), also emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation. Now 79 megawatts is not a lot for a star, but it is certainly a respectable amount: For comparison, we’ve been able to reliably detect a mere 8 watts in the form of a radio signal from the Pioneer 10 spacecraft when it was roughly 80 times farther from the Earth than the Sun. So Dyson calculated what it would take to detect a single graviton event, i.e., an atomic transition caused by a captured graviton, from this radiation, using the entire Earth as a perfect graviton detector. His result: We’d see roughly one graviton every billion years. That is how weakly gravity interacts with matter. Concerning the second half of the question, no, we do not “believe” that gravitons exist. Belief is done in other places. Rather, we know that if the gravitational field is a quantum field much like electromagnetism, in the so-called perturbative limit (basically, when the field is weak) it would manifest itself in the form of discrete quanta, which we call gravitons. So detecting gravitons would confirm our suspicion that gravitation, too, is a quantum phenomenon. Conversely, if we had a firm prediction that gravitons should be detected in a given experiment, and we failed to see those gravitons, that would at the very least falsify the idea that gravity is similar a a quantum field theory to electromagnetism. (Perhaps it is still a quantum theory, but something manifestly different.) The trouble is, we can do neither. We can neither detect gravitons nor reliably exclude their existence based on observations that we can do. So we end up speculating. There are plenty of theories out there, both quantum theories of gravitation and alternatives. Some are better than others, but we really have no way to decide which is right: without experiment, without observation, we are blind, and although we are reasonably clever monkeys, at no time in the history of science were we able to figure out something like this on our own, without hints from Nature as far as I know. How do objects bend or curve spacetime to produce gravity? They don’t. Seriously, they don’t. Don’t believe me? See if you believe this quote: “It is wrong to think that 'geometrization' is something essential. It is only a kind of crutch [Eselsbrücke] for the finding of numerical laws. Whether one links 'geometrical' intuitions with a theory is a ... private matter.” You know who wrote this? A chap who went by the name A. Einstein*. Objects, indeed all material fields with a nonvanishing stress-energy-momentum tensor, serve as sources of the gravitational field. The gravitational field interacts with matter universally and minimally. Universal, in this context, means that the actual material constitution of matter makes no difference; the gravitational field does not care what matter is made of, only its stress-energy-momentum. Minimal, in this context, means that the interaction is confined to a mathematical form that determines inner products and volume elements and nothing else. A field that interacts with matter minimally can be reinterpreted using the language of covariant derivatives as geometry. Usually, this geometry depends on the material properties of matter; e.g., for electromagnetism, this geometric interpretation depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the matter particle involved. Not so in gravity: Because it is universal, the “gravitational charge-to-mass ratio” is the same for everything, so the geometry is universal. But that means that everything is subject to this geometry, including our senses and our instruments. It is the only geometry that can be observed, so we can elevate this to a principle, or interpretation, and suggest that gravitation determines the geometry of spacetime. Whether or not we should think of gravitation this way is another matter. Gravitation is more than geometry. The gravitational field has a physical existence. It carries energy and momentum in the form of gravitational waves, just as the Maxwell field carries energy and momentum in the form of electromagnetic waves, such as light. Einstein understood this, hence his advice not to take the geometric interpretation as dogma. Matter does not “bend or curve spacetime”. Matter is the source of the gravitational field. This gravitational field affects everything universally, including any attempt to detect the geometry of spacetime. But spacetime is not a physical thing; matter and the gravitational field are physical things. *Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926, as translated by Lehmkuhl, in Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326, DOI: 10.1016/j.shpsb.2013.08.002 If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? A black hole does not have immense strength or infinite density. Mostly, no infinite gravity either. Take a black hole that has the same mass as the Sun. Put it in place of the Sun. Guess what happens to the Earth? Apart from the lack of sunlight (which would be bad news for us humans) absolutely nothing. The gravity of that black hole is exactly the same, finite gravity as that of the Sun. Density? Sure, a stellar sized black hole is dense. Actual black holes do not form at a mass much less than about three times the mass of the Sun. But even neutron stars are insanely dense, many trillions of times denser than water. But… this may come as a surprise but very, very large black holes are not so dense at all! When we talk about the largest supermassive black holes, they can form at densities less than the density of ordinary water. It’s only when the black hole is relatively small (by that, I mean, three times the mass of the Sun, which would be “only” a million times the mass of the Earth) that such insane densities are encountered as matter collapses into a black hole. And then, the gravity. As I said, at the same distance as the Sun, a one solar mass black hole has the same gravity as the Sun. Far from infinite. So let’s get a little closer. In the case of the Sun, the closest we can get to its center is about 700,000 kilometers, before we collide with the Sun’s surface. At that distance, solar gravity is powerful (about 30 times the gravity of the Earth at sea level) but far from infinite. And you cannot get any closer, because now you would be inside the Sun. But now take that black hole. A black hole with the same mass as the Sun has an effective radius of only about 3 kilometers. Going from 700,000 to 3… as you know, gravitational acceleration is proportional to the inverse square of distance. So now we are up to trillions of times Earth gravity! And that’s just the Newtonian result. Once we take relativity theory into account, there is, after all, one infinity to deal with. At exactly the event horizon, you would literally need an infinitely powerful rocket exerting an infinite force to hover. But that’s because the event horizon has this strange spacetime geometry: “hovering” means the same thing as moving at the vacuum speed of light. Which, as we know, is not possible without an infinitely powerful rocket. But anywhere outside the event horizon, gravity is finite. And it’s strong not because the black hole’s gravity is stronger than the gravity of another object of the same mass, but simply because you can get that much closer to it. As another example, take the Earth. Its radius is roughly 6,370 kilometers or just under 4,000 miles. The radius of a black hole of the same mass? Less than 9 millimeters. Just over one third of an inch. Imagine something with a diameter of two thirds of an inch, not larger than what one of my cats would produce when he is constipated, a pebble really, that weighs as much as the entire planet Earth. What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? Very simple: Direct detection. The existence of dark matter is widely assumed, as we observe gravitational behavior that cannot be explained otherwise within the context of general relativity: the same general relativity that, on other scales (e.g., within the solar system) works with spectacular precision. Now of course just because something works on a size scale measured by light-hours at most does not mean that it will necessarily work equally well on a size scale measured in the thousands or tens of thousands of light-years or more. Which means that there may not be dark matter at all: perhaps the laws of gravitation must be modified! But that proves to be an immensely tricky thing to do, because most modifications run into other observational constraints. Gravitational radiation, arrival times of gravitational and non-gravitational signals from the same event, cosmological observations… the bar is set very high for such modified theories of gravity. But until we have direct confirmation of dark matter, we won’t know for sure. And so far, all we have are null results: None of the attempts to search for dark matter by nongravitational means proved successful. So the jury is still out. Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? To move forward in space, you don’t need to do anything. Once a body is in motion, it remains in motion unless a force acts upon it… and in space, no such forces are usually present. However, if you want to accelerate a body, things change. Acceleration means a change in the body’s momentum. But momentum is one of those quantities that are always strictly conserved. So if you change the momentum of a body, the momentum of something else, somewhere, must change by an equal but opposite amount. Reaction mass could be that something else. This is how rockets work. However, if you find something outside of your space vehicle, perhaps you can change its momentum without throwing anything away. For instance, here in the vicinity of the Earth, you might be able to interact with the Earth’s magnetic field and accelerate; in exchange, the Earth itself would accelerate in the opposite direction, but given how much more massive the Earth is compared to a spaceship, this change in the Earth’s momentum is imperceptible. It might be possible to repeat the feat on larger scales, using, e.g., the magnetic field of the Sun or even galactic magnetic fields, albeit these fields are very weak so the sheer size of whatever equipment might accomplish this miracle likely makes the concept impractical. It is also possible to make use of the momentum of something already there, e.g., sunlight. Or the momentum of something we put there ourselves, e.g., light from a powerful ground-based laser. In both cases, the spacecraft would have a lightsail that, as it interacts with (and changes the momentum of) the light it receives, imparts a momentum on the spaceship that carries it. There is also gravitational assist: When there are at least two bodies in a system (and there are certainly more than two bodies here in the solar system) it is possible to follow a trajectory that changes direction with respect to one of the bodies, but changes direction and magnitude of velocity with respect to the other. Again, momentum is conserved: the motion of the bodies involved also changes. But again, bodies such as planets in the solar system are so much heavier than a spaceship, any change in their momenta will remain imperceptible. Throughout it all, however, the common theme is that books must always remain balanced when it comes to momentum. If your spaceship accelerates in some direction, something else — propulsion mass, a planet, rays of light, whatever — must accelerate in the opposite direction. How do scientists detect dark matter if it does not interact with light or other forms of matter except through gravity? How is it possible to observe something that does not emit light? To date, dark matter has not been detected. Its existence is inferred from the gravitational behavior of visible structures, but it has not been confirmed by direct detection, despite numerous attempts to do do. These failures do not mean that dark matter doesn’t exist, but they did exclude several plausible theoretical models. Meanwhile, precisely because dark matter’s existence has not yet been directly confirmed, the door remains open to viable alternatives, in the form of modified theories of gravitation that do away with the need for dark matter in the first place. However, this is not as easy as it sounds. The “dark matter paradigm” fits the data reasonably well. Modifying the theory of gravitation comes with unexpected consequences. Einstein’s theory works at very high precision here in the solar system; a modified theory of gravitation would have to reproduce these results. Dark matter does a decent job at producing data consistent with the large-scale structure formation (gravitational “clumping”) of matter; most theories of gravitation run into trouble. LIGO observations confirm that gravitational waves and light travel at the same speed; many modified gravity theories would predict something different and are therefore excluded. And the dark matter model accurately reproduces the statistical fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background, another difficult challenge for modified gravity. That is not to say that the standard dark matter model does not have its own share of difficulties, ranging from the famous Hubble tension (different values for the Hubble parameter when measured “locally” vs. inferred from cosmological observations) to the unexplained emergence of mature early galaxies and supermassive black holes in the early universe. So I daresay the jury is still out. We shall see what happens; dark matter is probably a safe horse to bet on, but its victory is by no means assured. Where can I find an explanation of the Standard Model Lagrangian that explains the meaning of each term? In a book. Specifically, let me recommend the book that, to me, is the “go to” reference on the Standard Model: The Standard Model, by Burgess and Moore (2007). Very elegantly, cleanly written, it systematically constructs the Standard Model Lagrangian from first principles, exploring the significance and properties of each term. In fact, it is thanks to this book that I resist the temptation to try and offer an explanation here, in the form of a short Quora answer. That is because I realize that the book, in a mere 500-odd pages, offers the most concise, yet sensible presentation of the model. Sure, I could copy-paste the LaTeX of that monster Lagrangian here just to show what a clever boy I am, but without the background, the details that are in the book, the symbols mean little. So rather than trying to impress folks with a nasty multiline equation occupying the better part of a full printed page, let me just recap its essence: It is a Lagrangian that incorporates an S U ( 3 ) c × S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) gauge theory of quarks and leptons, combined with the Higgs mechanism. Here, S U stands for the symmetry group of unitary matrices with positive determinant; these matrices can be used to represent families of particles with certain behavior. U ( 1 ) , similarly, is a rotation in the complex plane, again suitable to represent certain particles mathematically. The “gauge” nature of the interaction is represented by the fact that the force carried by the interaction is described mathematically using covariant derivatives. The S U ( 3 ) c part of the Lagrangian represents an interaction (the strong force) carried by a family of eight massless spin-1 particles (gluons). Particles that interact by way of exchanging these gluons are said to carry “color” charge. The S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) part corresponds to a family of four spin-1 particles. Here, the S U ( 2 ) part of the symmetry is “broken”, because of an additional interaction with a scalar field, the Higgs field. As a result, the three spin-1 particles mediating the S U ( 2 ) part (i.e., the weak interaction) are massive. The remaining, massless vector boson is the well known photon of electromagnetism. The particles that interact with these fields are fermions. They include fermions that participate in the strong force (quarks) and fermions that only participate in the electroweak interaction. Of these, the charged leptons such as electrons have electric charge; neutrinos do not. There is also the handedness of neutrinos that is encoded in the Lagrangian. This fermionic content is repeated three times to represent the three generations of quarks and leptons. Finally, the model is completed by a term that represents the Higgs field, with its peculiar potential and interactions with the other fields, which allow for the mechanism of symmetry breaking through which charged leptons and quarks also acquire masses. The strength of this model is that it yields a renormalizable (no crazy infinities) representation of all the known particle content of the universe, successfully predicting the outcome of many difficult experiments, indeed leading to the theoretical prediction, later confirmed experimentally, of the existence of particles like the Z-boson, the top quark, and last but not least, the Higgs boson. The specific form of the Lagrangian and the particle-content that it represents are all based on experimental evidence. Missing from the Standard Model is any mechanism to endow neutrinos with masses; any explanation as to why there are three generations of fermions; the nature of neutrinos vs. antineutrinos; and, of course, a proper unification with gravity. These omissions and the ways in which they might be addressed are also covered in the Burgess and Moore book. Well, that’s the gist of it. Beyond this, I think you really need a textbook or two. Burgess and Moore is great, but it assumes that you understand the basics of quantum field theory, so you might have to start somewhere else. The book, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory by Peskin and Schroeder, might be a good choice, it’s one of the best (if not the best) reasonably up-to-date textbooks out there. Classical physics says objects move because they were pushed. Quantum physics says objects tunnel spontaneously (and not pushed by anything). how can this difference be resolved? Actually, neither of the statements in the question are correct, but let me get down to details. Classical physics says that the motion of an object may change (i.e., it accelerates) if a force acts on that object. Motion requires no pushing. A change in motion requires pushing. This was historically not evident to humans until early modern times, since it seemed that, for all practical intents and purposes, motion ceased unless things were pushed continuously. It was not until Newton and others that we learned that this cessation of motion required a force as well: the force of friction, air resistance or other “dissipative” forces that turned the macroscopic motion of objects into the microscopic motion (rotation, vibration, etc.) of particles that we recognize as (waste) heat. What quantum physics says is not that “objects tunnel”. Nothing of the sort. Tunneling is about states, not objects. A system’s state may be characterized, among other things, by its energy-content. In classical physics, a system may lose energy to its environment if a lower energy state is available, but it does not happen if achieving that lower energy state first requires climbing to higher energy state, i.e., climbing over a (fictitious) “barrier”. This really should not be terribly mysterious. A piece of wood is in a higher energy state than the ashes and smoke that it turns into when it burns. Yet wood does not combust spontaneously. That is because its higher energy state is metastable. We need to invest energy (light it on fire with a match) in order to overcome the energy barrier before the wood can combust on its own and turn into ashes and smoke, with the excess energy released as heat. And this is what tunneling is about: a quantum system may overcome that barrier even in the absence of a push. We picture this as the system “borrowing” energy from the vacuum but I caution against reading this too literally. What it basically means is that something that is impossible in classical physics is simply improbable in the quantum world. However, and this must be stressed, the quantum world may be probabilistic in nature but conservation laws, including the law of energy conservation, are not. They hold exactly even in the world of quantum physics. That energy barrier? The system never exists as an observable system in a transitional state with more energy than it began with. The system can be observed before tunneling and after tunneling, with the released energy in some other form (again, for instance, waste heat).

Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them.
